## Observations

1. In a strictly increasing subsequence, the last element is the largest, so checking that it is at most X is enough.
2. For each attainable length in the current prefix, it suffices to store the smallest possible last element. These minimum tails are strictly increasing with length: removing the last element from a subsequence leaves a shorter one with a smaller tail.
3. When a new value arrives, only the first minimum tail greater than or equal to it can change. If no such tail exists, the new value extends the longest subsequence. An equal value cannot extend a strictly increasing subsequence.
4. Queries with the same R use the same minimum tails, so all queries can be answered during one left-to-right pass over the sequence.

## Solution sketch

> Queries with the same R use the same minimum tails, so all queries can be answered during one left-to-right pass over the sequence.

1. Group queries by R, keeping each query’s original index. Start with an empty list of minimum tails and scan the sequence from left to right. At position R, update the list with the current value before answering that group, so the queries include A_R.

> When a new value arrives, only the first minimum tail greater than or equal to it can change. If no such tail exists, the new value extends the longest subsequence. An equal value cannot extend a strictly increasing subsequence.

2. Binary-search for the first tail greater than or equal to the current value. Replace that tail, or append the value if the search reaches the end. The preceding tail, if present, is strictly smaller and can be extended by the new value; if there is no preceding tail, the new value starts a length-one subsequence. Shorter lengths already have smaller tails, and longer lengths cannot end at the new value because their predecessor lengths have no tail strictly smaller than it. This also handles an empty list and repeated values.

> In a strictly increasing subsequence, the last element is the largest, so checking that it is at most X is enough.

> For each attainable length in the current prefix, it suffices to store the smallest possible last element. These minimum tails are strictly increasing with length: removing the last element from a subsequence leaves a shorter one with a smaller tail.

3. For each query in the current group, binary-search for the first tail strictly greater than X. The number of tails before that point is the answer: a length is feasible exactly when its minimum tail is at most X. A tail equal to X counts, and if no tail exceeds X, the answer is the full list length. The input guarantee ensures that at least one tail qualifies. Store the answer at the query’s original index.

> Queries with the same R use the same minimum tails, so all queries can be answered during one left-to-right pass over the sequence.

4. Print the stored answers in input order. There is one binary search per sequence element and one per query, giving O((N + Q) log(N + 1)) time. The tails, query groups, and answers use O(N + Q) space.
